findings.assessment: The skill distinguishes producer/consumer data flow from mutation alone, explains same-wildcard capture and explicitly rejects equating two independent unknown element types.
findings.evidence: Unmodified extracted swap body works on a mutable list; an unmodifiable input rejects mutation. Independent wildcard capture and Double→Integer destination fail to compile for the expected bounds reasons. Double→Number copy preserves the original object.
findings.consequence: No need to add a universal wildcard rule or a cast-based workaround.

findings.assessment: The Attributes example checks insertion with Class.cast, gives exact-key replacement semantics, documents null/primitive-key and thread-confinement limits, and distinguishes assignable lookup from exact identity.
findings.evidence: Unmodified extracted class compiles cleanly. Raw String.class key plus Integer value throws before mutation and preserves the previous String. Exact/missing keys, replacement, null ambiguity and primitive-token rejection matched the written contract.
findings.consequence: No early-failure or multiplicity gap was found; changing the storage pattern would be gratuitous.

findings.assessment: TypeRef is already explicitly an illustration, not a production validated container. The text warns about mismatched Map values, unsupported/unresolved captures and mutable aliases.
findings.evidence: Unmodified extracted TypeRef distinguishes a concrete List<String> declaration token from a generic-method token whose argument remains TypeVariable T. List.class.cast accepts a List<Double>; it does not inspect elements.
findings.consequence: No reason to turn an intentionally partial capture illustration into an unsolicited token framework.

findings.assessment: Array covariance/reification, safe confinement and generic varargs assertions are qualified correctly; exposed array failures depend on the consumer's required runtime array class.
findings.evidence: Reifiable List<?>[] accepted; List<String>[] creation rejected. Object[] backed by String[] rejects an Integer store. Unsafe generic varargs fail at the caller cast. A leaked Object[] can satisfy an Object[] consumer but fails a String[] consumer. Overridable @SafeVarargs method rejected.
findings.consequence: No unsafe blanket SafeVarargs or unchecked-array recommendation needs correction.

findings.assessment: The package already warns that leftmost bound/erasure changes can break old binaries even when new source compiles, and requires old-source/old-binary checks.
findings.evidence: The same Client.java compiles against either interface-bound order. Changing Comparable-first to Serializable-first changes the descriptor; old client with new API fails NoSuchMethodError, while recompilation restores the tested call.
findings.consequence: Existing compatibility guidance is consequential and correct; retain it without restating a generic migration checklist.

findings.assessment: The Object-operand qualification for parameterized instanceof and var/diamond inference distinction match the target language rules.
findings.evidence: Object instanceof List<String> rejects; List<String> instanceof ArrayList<String> compiles. var new ArrayList<>() is accepted by an ArrayList<Object> consumer and allows the two deliberately different element types.
findings.consequence: No outdated blanket ban on all parameterized instanceof tests or inference claim was found.
